title: The battle between British and American English

entries.term: two nations separated by a common language
entries.note: A description of England and the United States supposedly coined by [[see:George Bernard Shaw]]; the hosts agree the two speak different versions of English, not different languages.
Supposedly the person who described England and America as [[see:two nations separated by a common language]].
The British word for what Americans call an [[equivalent:elevator]]; Rob prefers its single swift syllable, and Jess admits she likes it a little better.
The American word for a British [[equivalent:lift]]; Rob mocks it for having four syllables.
British for an [[equivalent:apartment]]; from Old English [[from:flet]], a dwelling, especially on the ground floor, with a Proto-Indo-European root suggesting an area spread out.
The American word for a [[equivalent:flat]]; Jess prefers it because it literally means a place apart, which Rob finds too long and too general.
British for fried potato strips, first found in A Tale of Two Cities; thin vegetable slices were called chips from 1769. Rob's chips are thicker than [[equivalent:french fries]].
From French fried potatoes (1856), as frying in fat was considered French; the story of First World War troops in Belgium naming them is debunked.
What Jess would call a thicker piece of fried potato, the kind Rob gets with fish and calls [[see:chips]].
One of the many American shapes of fried potato that all fall under the umbrella term [[see:french fries]].
One of the many American shapes of fried potato that all fall under the umbrella term [[see:french fries]].
One of the many American shapes of fried potato that all fall under the umbrella term [[see:french fries]].
British for what Americans call [[equivalent:potato chips]]; a young Rob in Orlando asked for [[see:chips]] and kept getting cold crisps.
The American term for British [[equivalent:crisps]], which Rob was given in Florida when he asked for chips and then for potato.
A nationalist American replacement for [[see:french fries]], tried around the start of the Iraq War when France disagreed with the US approach.
A 1950s wave of renaming [[see:french fries]], used for McDonald's-style fries for a while before the French name returned.
Means the backside in America but the female genitals in Britain; most likely from the novel [[from?:Fanny Hill]], though an earlier source is possible.
A 1748 novel, also called Memoirs of a Woman of Pleasure, named after a person; an early work of literary pornography that prompted obscenity debates and laws.
Author of [[see:Fanny Hill]], arrested in 1749 with his publishers and printer for corrupting the king's subjects.
American for [[equivalent:trousers]] but British for underwear; named after [[from:Pantalone]] via [[from:pantaloon]].
British for what Americans call [[equivalent:pants]]; for Jess it is a more specific word for smart business pants.
An American word for underwear which, like [[same-root:pants]], is named after the commedia dell'arte character [[from:Pantalone]].
Comes from the name of [[from:Pantalone]], the Italian character, and gave us [[gave:pants]].
A silly, greedy old commedia dell'arte character in red hose or leggings, mocked by women and servants, after whom [[gave:pants]] and [[gave:panties]] are named.
In Britain they hold up socks; in America they hold up pants, which the British call [[equivalent:braces]].
What Jess calls the thing that holds up socks, which in Britain is called [[see:suspenders]].
British for American [[equivalent:suspenders]]; to Jess it suggests an injury support, and in Britain a brace can also mean a pair, as in a brace of hares.
In Britain a sweet baked treat Americans call a [[equivalent:cookie]]; in much of the US a buttery, fluffy bread without yeast, closer to a [[see:scone]].
What an American [[see:biscuit]] most resembles; the hosts set aside its disputed pronunciation as another podcast.
A Southern dish Jess makes with the American [[see:biscuit]]; Rob says biscuits in gravy would be an abomination in Britain.
American for a British [[equivalent:biscuit]], also used in Britain for soft or chocolate-chip ones; from Dutch, entering English through Dutch settlers in America.
A kind of baked good, one of the Dutch words that entered English in the United States, like [[see:cookie]].
Another Dutch word that, like [[see:cookie]], entered English in the United States.
From German, entering English in the United States through immigrants living alongside one another.
An Italian word that entered English in America for the long green squash the British call [[equivalent:courgettes]].
The British name for what Americans call [[equivalent:zucchini]].
An American coinage from existing English words, inspired by small white varieties that look like eggs; the British call it an [[equivalent:aubergine]].
Rob's British word for what Americans call an [[equivalent:eggplant]].
An example of the Native American names settlers adopted for new things they encountered in America, like [[see:raccoon]].
From a Native American word meaning "he scratches with the hands", which echoes names in other languages, like German [[equivalent:Waschbär]].
The German word for [[equivalent:raccoon]]; most languages call it something like this, after the animal washing its food in water.
A word already used by other Europeans that American settlers took up, since Britain had no such thing or native word for it.
A word already used by other Europeans that American settlers took up for a landscape feature Britain lacks.
A word already used by other Europeans that American settlers took up for something Britain lacks.
Like [[see:eggplant]], an American name made by combining existing English words.
One of Jess's American words for waste, used in garbage truck and garbage can, where the British say [[equivalent:rubbish]].
Jess's other American word for waste, as in trash bag, with a British equivalent in [[equivalent:rubbish]].
The British word for waste put in the bin and collected by the bin man, where Americans say [[equivalent:garbage]] or [[equivalent:trash]].
Waste in the street, used more in Britain, where there are litter bins; for Jess it means only discarded waste on the ground.
In American English, the municipal worker who collects garbage, unlike a [[see:trash person]].
Not a name for a waste collector, unlike [[see:garbage person]], because it is an insult.
The American word for what Rob calls the [[equivalent:post]], although Rob's post is delivered by the Royal Mail and Jess's by the US Postal Service.
The British word for [[equivalent:mail]], though both countries call the building a post office.
Where Americans put letters, which the British call a [[equivalent:post box]].
The British word for an American [[equivalent:mailbox]].
The British term for what Americans call [[equivalent:phone booths]].
The American term for British [[equivalent:phone boxes]], of which few remain.
Spelled without the U in America thanks to [[see:Noah Webster]], which brings it closer to Latin; once spelled many ways, such as coolor and colur.
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.
One of the words, like [[see:color]], spelled with -our in Britain and -or in America.
Author of the first American English dictionary, who deliberately changed spellings like [[see:color]] and argued America needed its own language standard.
One of those [[see:Noah Webster]] consulted when changing American spellings.
American endings -ize and -yze contrast with British -ise and -yse, as in [[see:analyze]], [[see:paralyze]] and [[see:apologize]].
An example of the different British and American spellings of the [[see:-ize]] ending.
An example of the different British and American spellings of the [[see:-ize]] ending.
An example of the different British and American spellings of the [[see:-ize]] ending.
Spelled with two L's in Britain but one in America; Jess prefers the double L, since a single L suggests a long E.
Rob spells it with two G's, as did a New York pub called the [[see:Wagon and Horses]]; American English uses one.
A pub in New York where Rob used to drink, whose sign spelled [[see:wagon]] with two G's.
The hosts decided the podcast's name should have two L's, as in [[see:traveller]] and revelled, to avoid a long-E reading.
From French with a U that British English once had but dropped, unlike [[see:color]]; Jess wonders if the [[see:Reign of Terror]] put people off.
Jess guesses it may have put English speakers off the Frenchified spelling of [[see:terror]].
During it, vowel spellings were fixed at different points, so they reflect mismatched pronunciations, one cause of inconsistent English spelling.
The one word the US spells with -our, possibly due to French fashion, though in the 1700s it was spelled glamer.
Americans increasingly say "neesh", while "nitch" was more common in Jess's youth; Rob thinks ignoring the final E is an abomination.
Pronounced differently in America; Rob can tolerate the American version as it fits words like [[see:plaque]].
A word ending in -que that Rob says makes the American pronunciation of [[see:cliché]] seem acceptable.
Pronounced differently in the US and in British high society, showing that neither side consistently sticks closer to French.
The British pronunciation is far closer to French than the American one, which Jess doubts she will ever shake.
The British spelling gaol is justified by legal tradition, but neither spelling is superior, both coming from Late Latin [[from:caveola]], little cage.
Dismissed in Britain as a newfangled Americanism or accidental portmanteau, but it is a long-established word.
An American word that is older than the British [[equivalent:nappy]].
The British word for a [[equivalent:diaper]], which is actually the older usage.
A British myth says Americans prefer it over [[equivalent:titbit]] out of puritanism, but both forms are equally old.
The British form of [[equivalent:tidbit]], which Jess finds hilarious; Rob compares its tit- to the small bird [[see:titmouse]].
A very small bird whose name Rob compares with [[see:titbit]].
Avoided in Britain as an Americanism, though it has been around for a very long time.
British speakers dismiss it as an Americanism, but it is very old.
One of the playful, Latin-sounding words with nonsense elements coined by playwrights around 1800 and given to American characters like the [[see:Davy Crockett]] types.
The all-American type of character into whose mouths words like [[see:discombobulate]] were put.
Means to leave abruptly, combining the prefix ab-, away from, with squat, to sit or stay; a coinage like [[see:discombobulate]].
A playful coinage like [[see:discombobulate]], combining [[from:blow]] and [[from:orate]].
A deliberately overcomplicated version of [[from:obfuscate]], an example of swaggering American wordplay.
A playful coinage combining [[from:fluster]] and [[from:frustrate]].
Means to eat, a playful coinage based on [[from:scrumptious]].
One of the American English words now used on both sides of the Atlantic.
An American English word that comes up a lot and is now shared by both varieties.
An American contribution to English, one of many that seem to come from the movies.
An American contribution to English, one of many that seem to come from the movies.
An American contribution to English that sounds as if it came from crime films.
To hustle or be a hustler is an American contribution to English, like many crime-film-sounding words.
Its use for classified documents is an American take on the word.
Listed among the American English words now used in both countries.
In the sense of swindling someone, an American contribution to English.
Listed among the American English words now used on both sides of the Atlantic.
Its use for a restaurant, rather than a person who dines, is an Americanism.
Its use as a verb, to interview someone, is one of the noun-to-verb conversions English owes to America.
Its use as a verb, to divorce someone, is credited to American English.
To vacation somewhere is an American verb from a noun, matched in British English by to [[equivalent:holiday]] somewhere.
Used as a verb in British English, to holiday somewhere, as the equivalent of the American to [[equivalent:vacation]].
Now taken for granted in Britain, but listed as an Americanism to avoid in the Manchester Guardian's 1950 style guide.
As a verb, listed as an Americanism to avoid in the Guardian's 1950 style guide; Jess notes verbing nouns is a Shakespearean tradition.
Banned as an Americanism in the Guardian's 1950 style guide, which preferred going bald.
The Guardian's 1950 style guide ruled this construction out as American, preferring "have the aim of doing something".
The 1950 Guardian style guide demanded "help them to finish" instead, requiring the extra "to" of the infinitive.
Ruled out as an Americanism in the Guardian's 1950 style guide in favour of "so far", though now widely used in Britain.
